candidates.speaker: Stephen Boyce
candidates.proposition: Paul consistently understood Jesus as a physical Jewish man who died by Roman crucifixion and was later regarded as the resurrected Messiah.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Boyce the floor, and this uninterrupted opening-statement passage is delivered in the first person by him.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Paul is the earliest evidence discussed, so Boyce's claim that Paul already believed in an earthly, bodily Jesus directly supports historicity against the celestial-Christ hypothesis.
candidates.contextSummary: Boyce appeals to Paul's activity before and after conversion, Paul's descriptions of death, burial, crucifixion, Abrahamic descent, birth from a woman, and the resurrection as the change in Paul's evaluation of Jesus.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Boyce
candidates.proposition: Paul's designation of James as the brother of the Lord identifies a particular biological relative of Jesus rather than merely a fellow Christian.
candidates.attributionBasis: This passage continues Boyce's uninterrupted opening statement and develops his expressly introduced discussion of Paul meeting Peter and James.
candidates.loadBearingReason: A biological brother personally encountered by Paul would be strong early evidence that Jesus was an earthly person and would directly undermine a wholly celestial origin account.
candidates.contextSummary: Boyce argues that common names required distinguishing descriptions, compares Paul's naming of Cephas and James, and maintains that a generic Christian-brother reading would increase rather than resolve ambiguity.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Boyce
candidates.proposition: Josephus and other ancient writers used relational and titular descriptions to identify real people, supporting the biological reading of James as Jesus's brother.
candidates.attributionBasis: The same uninterrupted Boyce opening continues, with explicit transitions to Josephus, other writings, Tacitus, and Suetonius as supporting examples.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument supplies external linguistic and historical corroboration for Boyce's identification of James and Jesus, extending his case beyond an isolated interpretation of Paul.
candidates.contextSummary: Boyce invokes Josephus's description of James and Jesus, naming conventions in other writings, and Roman references to Christianity to argue that family connections, locations, and titles identified persons of interest.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Boyce
candidates.proposition: Hegesippus preserves a traceable dynasty of Jesus's physical relatives who led the Jerusalem church into the early second century.
candidates.attributionBasis: This is Boyce's final substantive premise in the same opening statement, explicitly introduced through Hegesippus and concluded before his overall summary.
candidates.loadBearingReason: A continuing family line attached to Jesus and early Jerusalem leadership would directly establish an earthly man with physical relatives remembered across generations.
candidates.contextSummary: Boyce cites traditions about Jude's grandchildren, imperial questioning of Jesus's relatives, and a succession of family leadership ending around 110 CE, then infers that Jesus was a real man with traceable relatives.

candidates.speaker: Richard Carrier
candidates.proposition: Jesus belongs to a wider class of suffering savior lords treated as historical despite being mythical, so his historicity requires exceptional evidence.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly transfers the floor to Carrier, and Carrier introduces this passage as the general thesis of his opening presentation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This establishes Carrier's central comparative prior: Christianity resembles other savior cults whose heroes did not exist, shifting the case toward requiring affirmative evidence for Jesus as an exception.
candidates.contextSummary: Carrier compares Jesus with numerous ancient savior figures whose suffering defeated death and promised followers a blessed afterlife, arguing that similar narrative and cultic features do not establish a historical founder.

candidates.speaker: Richard Carrier
candidates.proposition: The earliest writings locate knowledge of Jesus in scripture and revelation, while their apparent references to birth and brothers remain allegorical or ambiguous.
candidates.attributionBasis: Carrier remains the sole speaker throughout his opening and explicitly introduces Paul and other contemporary documents as the earliest relevant evidence.
candidates.loadBearingReason: If the earliest sources never clearly place Jesus on earth or identify witnesses and biological relations, their evidentiary pattern supports Carrier's celestial-origin hypothesis over straightforward historicity.
candidates.contextSummary: Carrier argues that Paul received information through scripture and revelation, never mentions earthly disciples, treats being born of a woman within allegory, and uses brother language broadly enough to leave biological kinship uncertain.

candidates.speaker: Richard Carrier
candidates.proposition: The Gospels are late, anonymous, unsourced, mythically structured accounts whose claims receive no demonstrably independent historical corroboration.
candidates.attributionBasis: This passage is an uninterrupted component of Carrier's opening, transitioning explicitly from Paul's evidence to the first clear earthly narratives in the Gospels.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Carrier's overall conclusion depends on denying that the later narrative and historical sources independently establish Jesus, leaving no evidence sufficient to distinguish him from other mythical savior figures.
candidates.contextSummary: Carrier characterizes the Gospels as anonymous works written later in another language and land, argues that later historians relied on Gospel traditions or Christian informants, and concludes that this cannot independently establish Jesus.

candidates.speaker: Richard Carrier
candidates.proposition: Paul could believe Jesus possessed Jewish and Davidic flesh, died, and rose while still placing those events in a celestial drama known only through scripture and revelation.
candidates.attributionBasis: Carrier explicitly identifies this as clarification of his own peer-reviewed theory in response to how Boyce presented Carrier's position.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The clarification answers the historicist inference from bodily language by separating material embodiment from earthly location, preserving the celestial hypothesis despite Paul's references to flesh, death, and resurrection.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Boyce's opening treated Paul's references to flesh, crucifixion, burial, and resurrection as evidence that Paul believed in an earthly historical Jesus.

candidates.contextSummary: Carrier concedes several descriptions emphasized by Boyce but argues that Paul never locates the events on earth, attributes death and resurrection knowledge to scripture, and describes apostolic encounters only after resurrection.

candidates.speaker: Richard Carrier
candidates.proposition: The grammar and argumentative context of Galatians leave James's title brother of the Lord ambiguous and do not establish that he was Jesus's biological brother.
candidates.attributionBasis: Carrier explicitly names Boyce's argument and then conducts a sustained grammatical and contextual response concerning Paul's meeting with Peter and James.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Boyce makes James a principal early witness to Jesus's physical family, so preserving a non-biological reading removes one of the historicity case's most important Pauline anchors.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Boyce argued that Paul named James as brother of the Lord specifically to distinguish Jesus's biological relative from other men named James.

candidates.contextSummary: Carrier argues that Paul's Greek excludes James from the apostles in the immediate statement, says Paul names everyone he met to defend his independence, and concludes that the title could denote either biological kinship or a Christian category.
